title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
hook: a bee stays too long inside a lotus, and the petals close at dusk
carry: which sense has hold of you

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana: fear not, there's a way across, and nobody can eat your dinner for you: there's no one to free you but yourself. What small dose of the real thing did you take? Day nine hundred ninety-six.

A bee works its way deep into a lotus on a pond, late in the afternoon, drunk on the scent, and stays. And stays. The light goes gold, then gray. The petals begin to fold inward, slowly, the way lotuses close at evening, and the bee is still inside. The Vivekachudamani puts the bee in a short list of creatures, each one caught by a single sense. Then it turns to the reader and asks a question.
screen: `A BEE INSIDE A LOTUS.` → `THE PETALS CLOSE.` → `A LIST, AND A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. The deer, the elephant, the moth, the fish and the bee: these five die, each bound by one of the five senses, sound, touch, form, taste and smell. What then of a person, bound by all five? The old explanations fill in each picture. The deer is drawn by a hunter's music. The elephant by touch. The moth flies into the flame it can't stop looking at. The fish takes the bait for the taste. And the bee stays in the closing lotus for the smell. Each one is ruined by something good. Music, touch, light, food, fragrance. None of them is evil. That's the sharp edge of the verse. It doesn't say the senses are wicked. It says a creature pulled along by even one of them can lose everything, and asks what happens to someone pulled by all five at once. Notice where this sits in a book about jnana. You might expect a book about knowing to stay in the head. But this verse brings the book right down to the body: what you look at, what you reach for, where your attention gets towed. On this path, discernment isn't only a thought about what lasts. It's noticing, in the moment, which sense has hold of you, and whether you chose it. The moth doesn't decide anything. It just flies. A person can notice the pull before the wings move. That noticing is a small, practical kind of knowing, and the text treats it as part of the road to the larger kind.
screen: `DEER, ELEPHANT, MOTH, FISH, BEE.` · `EACH CAUGHT BY ONE SENSE.` · `WHAT OF ONE CAUGHT BY ALL FIVE?` · `NOTICE THE PULL BEFORE THE WINGS MOVE.` · then, large: `WHICH SENSE HAS HOLD OF YOU?`

segments.voice: Let the body settle. Go through the senses one at a time, slowly, the way the verse lists them. Sound: whatever is in the room. Touch: the weight of the body on the seat. Form: the light behind your eyelids, or the room if your eyes are open. Taste: what's on the tongue right now. Smell: the air. Then ask, quietly, which of these pulls at you most. Don't push it away. Just see it. If you pray, you can offer that sense back as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing that frees. In the Vivekachudamani it starts small: seeing which sense has hold of you, before it carries you off.
Your line: which sense has hold of you. Today, the next time you reach for your phone, a snack or a song, pause one breath and name the sense that's pulling. Day nine hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Some students of the Vivekachudamani memorize short verses like this one and recall them during the day, using them to notice where the senses are pulling attention.

match.prompt: each creature, one sense — tap the pairs.

myth: the verse says the senses are wicked
each creature is ruined by something good: music, touch, light, food, fragrance. the danger is being pulled along.
the verse asks what happens to a person bound by all five senses
after the deer, elephant, moth, fish and bee, it asks: what then of a person bound by all five?

fork.setup: you're the moth. the flame is bright and warm. what can you do that the moth in the verse doesn't?
options: notice the pull before the wings move.
fork.reveal: the moth just flies. a person can notice which sense has hold of them, and the text treats that noticing as part of the road.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: indriya, a sense, the faculty of hearing, touch, sight, taste or smell.

trapdoor: what you thought: a book about knowing stays in the head.
what it means: the Vivekachudamani's knowing starts with seeing which sense has hold of you.
what a scholar hears: the verse of the five creatures, each bound by one sense, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, around verse 76.

notes: Index title/word/carry kept exactly; carry capitals come from the index title.
Verse 76 (shabdadibhih panchabhir eva pancha panchatvam apuh svagunena baddhah, kuranga-matanga-patanga-mina-bhringa narah panchabhir anchitah kim): confirm number and paraphrase.

The pairing of each creature with its sense and the 'old explanations' (deer drawn by music, elephant by touch, moth by the flame, fish by bait, bee by the closing lotus) are traditional glosses, not the verse itself; the script says so. Confirm the pairings.
'The bee in the closing lotus is an old picture in Indian poetry' is a general statement without a cited source; confirm or cut.
Day 999 (another writer) uses Ashtavakra's 'leave sense objects like poison'; this day avoids the Vivekachudamani's poison verse to keep them apart.
howItsDone says some students memorize short verses; confirm this is fair.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced 'an old picture in Indian poetry'; hook no longer opens with a time phrase that echoed day 992's 'Late in the evening'; 'warmth' corrected to 'touch' for the elephant so the list matches the verse's senses; 'keeps coming back to the body' (a claim about the whole book) narrowed to this verse; practice opener varied.

Audit: cut filler in the hook ('the picture isn't there to be sentimental about bees. It points at something'). Keeper note: the verses right after 76 are much sterner about sense objects (poison); the myth 'the verse says the senses are wicked' is about verse 76 only.
